title: LEADERSHIP: Dear Leader, You Need a Vacation
author: Business Leader Daily
summary: Josh at Business Leader Daily argues that leaders chronically postpone vacation by waiting for things to calm down -- a condition that never arrives. DDI's 2025 Global Leadership Forecast found that 71 percent of leaders reported increased stress, up from 63 percent three years prior, with more than half describing themselves as burned out. Americans left roughly 768 million vacation days unused in a recent year, with a third forfeited entirely. Leaders who never unplug model that pattern for their teams, eroding the people they spent years developing. Half-present vacation fails: even checking a few emails triggers work-related thinking for the rest of the day, so genuine recovery requires being fully offline. The leaders who sustain performance across decades are not those who grind every quarter but those who deliberately built rhythms of recovery into their work.
points: DDI 2025 data: 71% of leaders report increased stress; over half describe themselves as burned out -- both figures rising.
Americans forfeited approximately one-third of their 768 million unused vacation days in a recent year.
Leaders who never rest model that pattern for their teams, burning out the people they invested years building.
Checking even a few emails at the start of a vacation day restores work-related thinking for the entire remainder of the day.
Sustainable leadership performance requires built-in recovery rhythms, not willpower or grinding through every quarter.
quotes: Most leaders treat vacation as something they will get to once things calm down. Things never calm down.
If your default is to never take a break, your team quietly learns to emulate that pattern. They will work through their own breaks and arrive at the next big push already running on fumes.
I have found that even checking 'just a few quick emails' to start the day leads to thinking about work issues for the rest of the day.
The weight of leadership is real. But the weight you never put down is the weight that can eventually break you.
The leaders who stay sharp across decades did not white-knuckle through every quarter. They built rhythms of recovery into the work itself.
